title: Turkish Coffee & Tea Culture: How to Order Like a Local
seoTitle: Turkish Coffee & Tea Culture: How to Order Like a Local
metaDescription: Learn sade, orta and şekerli Turkish coffee orders, why tea comes in tulip glasses, Istanbul's historic coffeehouses, and authentic gift packs.
quickAnswer: Ordering coffee and tea in Türkiye follows clear local rules. Specify your Turkish coffee sweetness before it is brewed—sade (unsweetened), orta (medium), or şekerli (sweet)—because sugar is cooked into the pot. Drink Black Sea çay from narrow-waisted tulip glasses, brewed strong in a double teapot and diluted to your preferred shade.

body.text: What is the difference between sade, orta and şekerli Turkish coffee?

Because sugar is stirred into cold water and finely ground coffee inside the cezve (brewing pot) before heating, you must state your sweetness level when ordering. Sade means zero sugar, az şekerli adds half a teaspoon, orta adds one teaspoon for balanced body, and şekerli adds two teaspoons for a dessert-like cup.

Recognized on the [UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage list](https://ich.unesco.org/en/RL/turkish-coffee-culture-and-tradition-00645) since 2013, Turkish coffee is unfiltered and brewed slowly so a dense layer of foam (köpük) rises to the top. Never stir the cup once it lands in front of you—stirring kicks up the fine sediment (telve) resting at the bottom. Take a sip of the accompanying glass of plain water first to cleanse your palate, sip slowly, and stop before the last gritty spoonful.

body.text: Why is Turkish tea served in tulip glasses rather than mugs?

Turkish tea (çay) is poured into slim-waisted tulip glasses (ince belli) for heat control, comfort, and color inspection. The narrow waist keeps the lower half piping hot while the flared rim cools the top sip, lets your fingers grip the glass without a handle, and reveals the prized tavşan kanı ("rabbit's blood") crimson hue.

Inscribed by [UNESCO as the Culture of Çay](https://ich.unesco.org/en/RL/culture-of-cay-tea-a-symbol-of-identity-hospitality-and-social-interaction-01685) in 2022, Turkish black tea is grown primarily along the misty Black Sea slopes of Rize. Locals brew it in a stacked double kettle (çaydanlık): loose leaves steep slowly in the top pot while plain water boils below. When ordering, you control strength simply by asking for açık (light, more hot water), normal, or demli / koyu (dark and strong). Expect tea at breakfast, after lunch, on ferries, and inside every shop—declining a glass is never rude, though accepting one slows the day down in the best way.
Where are Istanbul's historic coffeehouses worth visiting?

Skip overpriced tourist cafés along Sultanahmet's tram line and head to working Istanbul institutions where locals still queue daily. Prioritize [Mandabatmaz](https://diginistanbul.com/beyoglu/place/cafe-coffee-shop/mandabatmaz/) off İstiklal Avenue for impossibly thick foam, [Fazıl Bey'in Türk Kahvesi](https://diginistanbul.com/kadikoy/place/cafe-coffee-shop/fazil-beys-turkish-coffee/) in Kadıköy market for freshly roasted blends, and [Kurukahveci Mehmet Efendi](https://www.mehmetefendi.com/eng/about-us/history) in Eminönü to buy hot-off-the-mill grounds.

items: Mandabatmaz (Beyoğlu): Tucked into Olivya Geçidi, its name literally means "the water buffalo wouldn't sink"—a nod to the density of its coffee foam. Low stools, zero pretense, and consistently tight technique.
Fazıl Bey'in Türk Kahvesi (Kadıköy): Operating in the Asian-side market since the 1920s, it roasts and grinds on site and serves classic damla sakızlı (mastic-infused) coffee alongside plain brews.

Kurukahveci Mehmet Efendi (Eminönü): Founded in 1871 near the Spice Bazaar, this is a retail roastery rather than a sit-down café. Join the fast-moving window queue for warm 100 g paper packets ground minutes earlier.
Çorlulu Ali Paşa Medresesi (Beyazıt): An 18th-century courtyard near the Grand Bazaar where you can sit under stone arches with a pot of tea or coffee away from street noise.

body.text: What coffee and tea packs make genuine gifts?

Skip glossy airport souvenir tins filled with stale, pre-flavored powder. Buy freshly ground 100 g vacuum or paper-wrapped packets from Kurukahveci Mehmet Efendi (or small-batch Kadıköy roasters) and loose-leaf Black Sea tea from [ÇAYKUR](https://www.caykur.gov.tr/Pages/lang/Design/WebForm2.aspx?Lan=1)—specifically Rize Turist, Altınbaş, or Organik Hemşin—paired with a heavy tin-lined copper cezve.

Watch out for "apple tea" (elma çayı) sold in tourist bazaars. Locals almost never drink sugary instant apple granules at home; it is largely a hospitality shortcut for foreign shoppers. If you want an herbal gift that Turks actually brew, pick dried ıhlamur (linden blossom) or adaçayı (Anatolian sage) from a neighborhood aktar (spice herbalist). Pair your coffee with a quick read of our [Turkish carpet and craft buying guide](https://itineraryofturkiye.com/blog/buying-carpet-in-turkey-tips) before shopping in Eminönü or the Grand Bazaar.

faq.q: Can I ask for milk in Turkish coffee?
faq.a: Traditional Turkish coffee is served black without milk. A regional exception is sütlü Türk kahvesi (brewed with milk instead of water), which you can request specifically at some cafés.

faq.q: Why is a piece of Turkish delight served with coffee?
faq.a: A single cube of lokum (Turkish delight) balances the roasted bitterness of sade or orta coffee and echoes Ottoman hospitality customs.

faq.q: How much does a glass of Turkish tea cost in Istanbul?
faq.a: At neighborhood tea gardens and Bosphorus ferries, a tulip glass of çay costs very little—often a fraction of a specialty espresso—while sit-down cafés with Bosphorus views charge a modest service premium.

faq.q: Is Turkish coffee stronger in caffeine than espresso?
faq.a: Per small 60 ml cup, Turkish coffee typically delivers roughly similar caffeine to a single shot of espresso, though the unfiltered brew feels heavier on the palate.

faq.q: Can you brew Turkish coffee at home without a copper cezve?
faq.a: Yes. Any small stainless-steel or brass long-handled pot works, provided you use ultra-fine powder-grade grind and keep the heat low so the foam builds gradually.

faq.q: Should I drink the grounds at the bottom of the cup?
faq.a: No. Let the cup rest for 30 seconds after it arrives so the grounds settle, then stop sipping once you reach the thick layer at the base.
